newsitem.title: USA: Locals not always told of SEC yield burning probes.
newsitem.headline: Locals not always told of SEC yield burning probes.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission does not by policy notify states and localities that it is investigating yield burning in their transactions, SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt told a U.S. House member.

But since SEC enforcement staff typically will ask the municipality involved for records, issuers may become aware of a probe, Levitt told Rep. Edward Markey, D-Mass., a member of the House finance subcomittee.
Levitt was responding to a series of written questions from Markey following a recent subcommittee hearing on SEC funding levels.

Markey asked, for instance, "Does the SEC promptly inform state or local governments (which) may have been the victims of yield burning abuses of the existence of an inquiry, so that they can take appropriate steps to addess tax consequences?"
Markey also asked what the SEC is doing to coordinate its yield burning enforcement activities with those of the IRS.

"The Commission has no specific policy concerning notification to issuers about allegations of yield burning," Levitt responded. "It is for the Internal Revenue Service to determine whether there will be tax consequences."
Levitt said the IRS code forbids the Service to disclose taxpayer return information to another government agency, like SEC, without a court order or taxpayer okay.
As a result, SEC generally does not know whether IRS is examining a transaction for yield burning or what IRS conclusions are, Levitt said.
"Effective coordination of individual investigations is difficult," Levitt said. "The ability to coordinate respective enforcement efforts ... is limited."

But Levitt said that in any SEC yield burning probe, the agency usually seeks information from all parties, including issuers. Thus "issuers may become aware of those allegations as a result of a Commission investigation," Levitt said.
Markey also wanted to know if SEC is monitoring the National Association of Securities Dealers' scrutiny of yield burning among its members.

Levitt said a review of NASD exam guidelines shows that while NASD routinely examines firms for excessive markups, it does not regularly review specifically for yield burning. SEC staff discussed coordinating their efforts at a recent meeting with NASD and more meetings are scheduled, he added.
SEC's chairman said the commission has, to date, brought no yield burning charges against muni market dealers.
But he noted that SEC alleged in two 1995 enforcement actions that a muni underwriter got undisclosed commissions and other payments from sellers of securities used for reinvestment.
The actions were against Stifel, Nicolaus and Co Inc and three of its officers, including Robert Cochran.

SEC charged that the payments created an "undisclosed risk" to the tax-exempt status of the bonds, Levitt said. In failing to disclose that risk, the underwriter and three officers defrauded bondholders, he said.

Stifel settled the SEC charges with a $1.4 million payment and the case against the officers is pending, Levitt said. Meanwhile, Cochran was convicted of criminal charges in May 1996, but the conviction was overturned recently by the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, Levitt noted.
Levitt said many issues surrounding yield burning, such as arbitrage limits and fair market value, fall under IRS' jurisdiction.
But yield burning may involve violations of the antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws too, he said.
For instance, if Treasury securities are sold at greater than fair market value, the seller may have violated the antifraud provisions by charging fraudulently excessive markups, Levitt said.

Also, muni bond investors may have been defrauded if a firm fails to disclose material facts about the purchase price of the reinvestment securities and the risk that bonds could be found to be arbitrage bonds and, therefore, not tax exempt, Levitt said.
